newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa January reserves data was leaked - dealers.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa January reserves data was leaked - dealers.

text.p: January reserves data was leaked well ahead of its official release time on Friday, in the latest example of insider trading which some fear may undermine South African markets' reputation, dealers said on Monday.
Traders at various banks said they had heard the figure at least an hour ahead of its 1600 GMT official release time. Others said the data had been leaked as early as Friday morning.
Traders say such leaks are now a routine event in the market and could hamper the government's plans to delegate its market-making activities from the Reserve Bank to private institutions.
Some observers warn that leaking sensitive data could also turn away new entrants to the South African market, if they get the impression they will not be dealing with a level playing field.
An hour before the January reserves data was officially released, Reuters received calls from market players quoting the figure. The reserves were officially released at 6 p.m. (1600 GMT).
The data, which showed reserves rose 1.46 billion rand to 11.76 billion rand in January, beat the most optimistic forecasts of 11.5 billion rand.
"I got a call on Friday at 4 p.m. and I was told a figure -- 11.8 billion -- that was within 40,000 rand of what came out," said one trader who asked not to be named.
While reluctant to identify companies, dealers say a handful of broking firms are named repeatedly when there is a suspicion that data has been leaked.
Little is done about the problem, despite repeated complaints to the relevant authorities, because there are no laws which can be used to prosecute successfully and because it is difficult to prove.
Reserve Bank deputy governor James Cross said he had been approached on the subject only once since joining the bank at the beginning of the year.
"I have had one discussion with one bank who mentioned that this was a problem that occurred from time to time," Cross said.
Central Statistical Services officials were not immediately available for comment. Dealers say, however, that virtually every important statistic is leaked regularly.
The issue was raised at a market-making workshop on Friday attended by Reserve Bank and Department of Finance officials and bond traders.
"It is one of the basic principles that we will not become market-makers if this problem is not addressed," said one senior trader who attended the meeting.
Government has said it plans to appoint formal market-makers in its stock in the bond market to allow the Reserve Bank, which is its current market-maker, to focus its attention on monetary policy.

Nedcor chief economist Dennis Dykes said that coupled with the fact that the problem of leaks put many local players at a disadvantage, it could also dissuade potential new foreign entrants to the South African market.
"If new entrants think they are not dealing with a situation where the playing fields are level...it is clearly not desirable," he said. "It is damaging and it sullies the country's reputation."

A government-appointed task group on insider trading is due to release its recommendations within the next four weeks, although legislation is only likely to be passed at the end of the year or early 1998.

In addition to clamping down on leaks of price-sensitive information on companies, task force chairman Mervyn King told Reuters recently he also wanted the law widened to include abuse of information about economic indicators.
Analysts suggest that one way of addressing the problem could be to reduce the number of people who have access to the data before its release.
For example, as many as 12 people handle the reserves data before its release, according to a Reserve Bank official.
Dykes also suggested that the U.S., where leaks of economic indicators are virtually unheard of, be studied as an example of curbing the problem.
